author: harness:claude-code

patch.value: Both token gates are structurally unable to fail: one measures only help payloads, the other measures command output against a three-item fixture, so no check anywhere compares real output to the ceiling the contract declares

The project declares a per-command output token ceiling in the contracts table and runs two gates named after token cost, and neither gate can observe a command exceeding its ceiling. Both were shipped by closed work that is otherwise correct; the defect is what they measure, not whether they exist.

Gate one, scripts/release/token-budget-gate.mjs, invoked as quality:token-budget and inside quality:static.

  - seedFixture (:51) creates exactly three items in an isolated temporary PM_PATH.
  - commandCorpus (:127) measures 17 surfaces against that three-item workspace.
  - The oracle is scripts/release/token-budgets.json, whose numbers are recorded observations of that fixture, not the contract-declared ceilings. list-default is budgeted at 649 bytes because three items produce 649 bytes.
  - The comparison at :230 is measurement.bytes against budget.max_bytes. default_max_estimated_tokens is never read. The contract ceiling is not this gate's oracle in any form.
  - The corpus omits every surface that actually overruns: activity, deps, graph, duplicates, events, and bare health are all absent.
  - It runs in nightly.yml:92 and release.yml:107 through quality:static. It does not run in ci.yml, so no pull request is gated on command output size.

Measured consequence, same command, same build, different workspace scale:

  pm list on the 3-item fixture      649 bytes    (gate budget: 649, passes)
  pm list on this repository      56,937 bytes    (87.7x the gate budget, unobserved)

The gate reports "Token budget gate passed (17 surfaces checked)" on a machine where pm activity emits 1,591,219 estimated tokens against a declared 4,000. It is structurally incapable of failing for the reason it exists, because output size on this surface is a function of workspace scale and the fixture has no scale.

Gate two, scripts/measure-agent-token-surface.mjs against scripts/agent-token-surface-baseline.json, invoked as quality:token-surface and chained into quality:context-eval, which does run on every CI pull request.

  - The committed baseline contains root_help, per_command_total, full_help_surface, three contracts payload sizes, mcp_tools_list, and a required_commands array that is a list of command names.
  - Every measured value is a help, contracts, or MCP registration payload. Not one is the output of a command doing work.

So the surface that is gated on pull requests measures only discovery cost, and the surface that measures command output is both fixture-bound and off the pull-request path. Between them there is no point in the pipeline where a command's real output is compared against the ceiling its contract declares.

Contract-declared ceilings are therefore decorative on both sides: not enforced at runtime, and not the oracle of either gate. That is why the 397.8x, 11.6x, 5.5x and 3.6x overruns measured on this workspace all shipped without a single failing check.

This is the same defect class as pm-lpqln4, where the only Bun coverage in the pipeline passes with an arbitrary token in the executable position: a gate whose passing carries no information. Recording the class explicitly matters more than either instance, because the remedy is a shared one -- a gate must be built with a negative control that proves it fails when the property it guards is violated.

Relationship to neighbours. pm-5t33or is the forward-looking feature that makes ceilings binding at runtime and its acceptance criteria already require extending the corpus gate; this item is the measured present-tense defect that motivates it and supplies the negative control that criterion needs. pm-cu1i and pm-dpqa3h are the closed items that shipped these two gates, and neither is wrong about what it delivered. pm-a22j is the original baseline measurement. The individual overruns each have their own owner and are not re-filed here.

The output-budget gate compares measured command output against the contract-declared default_max_estimated_tokens, not against a self-recorded byte snapshot; The gate corpus is measured against a workspace large enough that an unbounded surface exceeds its ceiling, and it includes activity, deps, graph, duplicates, events and bare health; A negative control proves the gate fails when a command is deliberately made unbounded, so a passing run carries information; The output-budget gate runs on every pull request, not only in nightly and release; The help and contracts payload baseline stays a separate declared measurement so discovery cost and answer cost are never conflated; Documentation states which gate owns discovery cost and which owns answer cost, and neither claims the other's coverage

message: Filed from reading both gates at HEAD and running them. token-budget-gate.mjs seeds 3 items (:51), measures 17 surfaces (:127), compares bytes to a recorded manifest (:230) that never reads the contract ceiling, and omits every overrunning surface; it runs only via quality:static in nightly.yml:92 and release.yml:107. agent-token-surface-baseline.json contains only help/contracts/MCP payload sizes. Measured contrast: pm list is 649 bytes on the fixture and 56,937 bytes here, 87.7x, unobserved. Duplicate check: pm-cu1i and pm-dpqa3h are the closed items that shipped these gates and describe delivery, not blindness; pm-5t33or is the runtime-enforcement feature; pm-lpqln4 is the same class on the Bun gate. None owns this.

author: harness:claude-code

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
A gate that has never failed is a hypothesis, not a guarantee, and the cheapest way to test it is to ask what workspace it measures.

Both gates this project named after token cost pass on every run and always have. Neither can fail. One measures a three-item fixture, where no surface can exceed a budget derived from that same fixture; the other measures help text, which does not vary with workspace size at all. The property both were built to protect -- that command output stays bounded as a workspace grows -- is precisely the property neither observes, because both were built at a scale where it cannot be violated.

The generalizable test: for any gate, name the input that would make it fail, then check that the input is reachable in the corpus the gate actually runs against. If it is not, the gate is measuring something else. This is the same shape as pm-lpqln4, where the only Bun coverage passes with an arbitrary token in the executable position, and the same shape as pm-ki67py, where a same-day release guard is correct only because no out-of-order tag happens to exist yet. Three instances in one project is a pattern, and the shared remedy is a negative control: a gate should ship with a proof that it fails when its property is violated.

The corollary for measurement generally: fixtures are for correctness, not for cost. Anything whose value scales with the data must be measured against data that has scale, or the number is about the fixture.

message: Durable lesson on gates that cannot fail, generalized from the three instances now recorded in this project.
